title: Micro-econ Tradecraft: Flash Lane for Sellers (Draft)
body:
Purpose
This is a compact, playbook-style reference for sellers and SEs to run fast counterfactual conversations about inference unit economics with platform engineers and procurement. Narrow focus: quick, evidence-led micro-economics statements + immediate fallback options that keep pilots shipping and revenue moving.

Intended audience
- Field sellers (SE + AE) running discovery and pilot conversion calls
- Platform/infra-focused SEs who need short scripts to translate latency/throughput needs into cost outcomes
- Ops-oriented sellers prepping for procurement or SRE stakeholder meetings

Core thesis (one-liner)
- Customers buy predictability and a predictable price for inference. Anchor every pilot on two numbers: expected p95 latency and projected per-1000-token cost. Then map 2 fallback levers (model variant, batching/cache) that preserve UX while lowering cost.

Structure of the flash lane (how to use this doc)
1) 45s opening (for quick discovery)
2) Rapid evidence snippets (benchmarks + customer analogies)
3) Objection playlets (technical + procurement)
4) Pilot guardrails and conversion checklist
5) Quick slide map (what to show in 3 slides)

1) 45s opening (voice + bullets)
- Opening (30s): "We help teams get consistent inference performance across environments, so you can predict costs and avoid surprise latency spikes during traffic growth. For pilots, we recommend locking two outcomes up-front: a p95 latency target and a per-1k token cost target. If we miss one, we trigger a graduated fallback.
- Quick qualification question (15s): "What SLOs and token counts are you modeling for peak? Example: 200 reqs/sec with avg 150 tokens per request?"

2) Rapid evidence snippets (use as pasteable talking points)
- Batching + KV cache example: "For chat workflows with repeated context, enabling KV cache typically cuts token compute by ~20–40% depending on prompt re-use. We can often hit a 2–3x cost reduction with minimal latency impact."
- Quantization note: "Switching to 4-bit quantization on compatible model families commonly reduces GPU memory footprint and per-token compute by ~1.6–2x; we preserve quality for classification and summarization but validate on an eval set for generation fidelity."
- Dedicated capacity promise: "Reserved pools remove noisy neighbor variance; customers at 5–10M tokens/day saw p95 drop by ~20–30ms and reduced tail risk during bursts."

3) Objection playlets (format: objection / empathy line / concrete reply / follow-up ask)
- Objection: "We can just self-host and save money."
  Empathy: "Totally — predictable unit cost is attractive."
  Reply: "Self-host often hides ops and calibration costs: kernel tuning, batching logic, cache invalidation, and SRE headcount. Our reserved model and compact runtime means most teams get to production faster and at a lower total cost-of-ownership for the first 12–18 months."
  Follow-up ask: "What internal ops bandwidth do you have for perf tuning and 24/7 incident response?"

- Objection: "We need enterprise security and can’t use hosted."
  Empathy: "Makes sense for regulated data."
  Reply: "We offer Private (VPC/on-prem) with KMS/HSM and audit logs. For pilots we can run a dedicated VPC instance to mirror production networking while keeping a single pane of ops."
  Follow-up ask: "Which compliance controls are must-haves for your legal team?"

- Objection: "Price is higher than X vendor."
  Empathy: "I hear you — procurement compares headline unit price."
  Reply: "Let’s compare apples-to-apples: show me the same p95 latency target and peak throughput. We optimize across 3 levers (batching, cache, quantization) and can often hit the same latency at lower steady-state token cost once prefix reuse stabilizes."
  Follow-up ask: "Can you share their SLA and example traffic shape?"

4) Pilot guardrails and conversion checklist (hands-on items to run a pilot that converts)
- Define SLO pair: p95 latency target + per-1k-token cost target (both numeric).
- Baseline run: 48–72h synthetic replay of expected traffic. Capture token length distribution and cold-start vs warm-state p95.
- Eval set: 200–500 prompts representative; run automatic quality regression checks (ROUGE/BLEU or embed-similarity thresholds).
- Fallback ladder: primary model -> quantized variant -> smaller model family with same prompt engineering. Define expected UX delta for each step.
- Ops handoff: schedule a 1-hour runbook review with their SRE and our SE before pilot kickoff.
- Acceptance criteria: pilot converts when cost target met for 7 continuous days without QoS regressions or when customer signs reserved capacity commitment.

5) Quick slide map (3 slides, 4 bullets each — minimal copy)
- Slide 1: Problem & Anchor
  - Problem: "Inference economics are hard to predict at scale"
  - Data point: "Typical pilot sees 2–4x token cost swings without caching/batching"
  - Ask: "Agree we should lock p95 + cost before pilot?"
  - Visual: simple bar chart (baseline vs cached vs quantized)
- Slide 2: How Redwood mitigates
  - Runtime optimizations (continuous batching, KV cache)
  - Routing + fallbacks (dedicated vs hosted vs private)
  - Measurable levers (batch size, cache TTL, quantization profile)
  - Visual: small flow with 3 levers and expected % cost delta
- Slide 3: Pilot plan & conversion path
  - 7–14 day pilot steps (baseline → optimize → convert)
  - Acceptance criteria (p95 + cost + quality)
  - Quick ROI math: tokens/day -> projected monthly spend -> estimated saving after optimizations
  - CTA: "Schedule a 30m pilot kickoff with infra + SE"

Pasteable snippets (for Slack / email)
- Short email opener: "Quick ask: can we lock p95 latency and a target per-1k cost for a 2-week pilot? We'll run a 48h baseline and propose 2 low-risk fallbacks if needed."
- Slack DM for platform engineer: "Can you share a replay or synthetic traffic shape (req/sec, median tokens, 95th tokens) so we can validate batch and cache profiles?"

Metrics / baseline numbers to keep in your toolkit (benchmarks — explain as ranges, not guarantees)
- Typical batching wins: 10–40% per-token compute reduction depending on request size distribution.
- KV cache hit improvements: 15–45% token compute saved for chat-like workloads where prefix reuse > 30%
- Quantization benefit: 1.5–2x throughput improvement for compatible models with minimal quality loss on classification tasks
- Tail improvements with dedicated capacity: p95 reduction of 10–30ms on average (higher at larger scales)

Open questions / TODOs (for the team)
- Validate new 20k-token long-context benchmarks for gpt-* family variants — ticketed as INF-5743.
- Create one updated slide with real customer numbers for caching wins (ask CS for anonymized example) — owner: Maya.
- Draft a short procurement comparison checklist that converts headline unit pricing into TCO over 12 months — owner: Rohit.

Quick checklist for SEs before a prospect call
- Bring these three numbers: expected peak req/sec, median tokens per request, p95 latency target.
- Ask for a replay or sample prompts.
- Prep two fallback choices (quantized model, smaller family) with expected UX delta.
- Prep acceptance criteria slide (3 lines).

Appendix: Short conversion math (pasteable)
- Inputs: tokens/day = avg_tokens_per_request * avg_reqs_per_day
- Baseline monthly cost = tokens/day * 30 * unit_price_per_1k_tokens/1000
- Projected savings = baseline - (baseline * optimization_delta) (use 20–40% as conservative range)

Example script (5-minute run)
- 0:00–0:45 Intro + anchor the problem (latency + cost unpredictability)
- 0:45–2:00 Quick qualification and show the three levers we’ll try
- 2:00–3:30 Baseline numbers and tradeoffs (draw a simple table)
- 3:30–4:30 Pilot plan overview and acceptance criteria
- 4:30–5:00 Close: ask for replay and schedule pilot kickoff

Notes to self (informal)
- Keep this doc short. Field teams want 1 page cheat + 3-slide deck.
- Avoid model brand FUD — emphasize mechanics (batching/cache/quant).
- Collect two short customer examples that show caching effect in production: one chat app, one classification pipeline.

End.
